notes.b: Matter is not created or destroyed, so the elements living things are built from have to be reused. Carbon is the clearest example: it moves round and round between organisms and their surroundings.
points: A biogeochemical cycle, or nutrient cycle, is the continuous movement of a chemical element between living things (bio) and the non-living environment (geo): the air, water, rocks and soil.

Matter is not created or destroyed, so the same atoms are used again and again. Energy, by contrast, flows through an ecosystem once and is lost as heat. There is more on this in Energy and nutrient transfer.

Carbon is the element at the centre of every biomolecule (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids; see Biomolecules and metabolism), so every organism needs a constant supply. Producers (organisms that make their own food, such as plants) take it in as CO₂; consumers get it already built into food.

A store (reservoir) is a place where carbon is held: the atmosphere (as CO₂, and a little methane, CH₄); living organisms (biomass, the mass of living material); dead organic matter in soil; the oceans (dissolved CO₂, hydrogencarbonate and carbonate); rocks such as limestone and chalk (calcium carbonate); and fossil fuels.
A process, or flux, is whatever moves carbon from one store to another. Stores are the boxes of the cycle and processes are the arrows between them.
CO₂ makes up only about 0.04% of the air (over 420 parts per million), yet it is the source of carbon for almost all life on Earth, because photosynthesis starts from it.
notes.tip: Define a nutrient cycle as movement of an element between living things and the non-living environment, and remember that matter is recycled while energy is not.

notes.h: Processes that remove carbon from the atmosphere
notes.b: Carbon dioxide leaves the air in only a few ways. By far the most important is photosynthesis, but dissolving in water and shell building also lock carbon away.
points: Photosynthesis by plants, algae and phytoplankton (tiny floating algae) fixes CO₂ into glucose and then into the rest of their biomass, so they act as carbon sinks (stores that take in more carbon than they release).
Photosynthesis is the only major route by which carbon enters living things, so nearly all the carbon in a food chain started as CO₂ taken in by a producer.
Dissolving: CO₂ dissolves in the surface of the oceans, lakes and rivers, and aquatic producers take it up for photosynthesis.
Shell and skeleton building: many marine organisms (e.g. corals, molluscs and some phytoplankton) combine dissolved carbonate with calcium to make calcium carbonate shells and skeletons.

When these organisms die, their shells and skeletons settle on the sea floor and, over millions of years, form limestone and chalk. These rocks are very long-term stores because the carbon stays locked in them for so long.
notes.tip: If asked to name processes that remove CO₂ from the air, give photosynthesis first, then dissolving in water and shell building.

notes.h: Processes that move carbon through living things
notes.b: Once carbon is in a producer it does not stay there. It passes along the food chain and into the dead matter that every organism leaves behind.
points: Feeding: carbon in the producer's biomass passes to herbivores and then carnivores when they eat and digest it. At each step most of it is respired away (broken down to release energy, giving off CO₂) rather than built into the consumer's body.
Each step in a food chain is a trophic level (a feeding level). There is more on this in Energy and nutrient transfer.

Egestion and excretion: carbon leaves animals in faeces and in wastes such as urea, and enters the dead organic matter store, as do shed leaves and dead organisms. This store is the food supply for decomposers.
notes.tip: Show feeding as an arrow from plants to animals, and death and excretion as arrows from both into dead matter.

notes.h: Processes that return carbon to the atmosphere
notes.b: Carbon dioxide is put back into the air by respiration, by decomposers, by burning and by geological release. If it were not returned, producers would run out of CO₂.
points: Respiration by plants, animals and microorganisms breaks down glucose and releases CO₂. Details are in Respiration as a catabolic process.

Plants respire all the time, day and night, so the respiration arrow must start from plants as well as animals. Over a growing season photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so the plant as a whole gains carbon.
Combustion: burning biomass (wood, peat, forest fires) or fossil fuels combines the carbon with oxygen and releases it as CO₂ very quickly.
Natural geological release: volcanoes release CO₂ from rocks, and the weathering of limestone releases some. This is small compared with the biological fluxes and with fossil-fuel burning.
notes.tip: Name the processes that add CO₂ to the air as respiration (in plants too), decomposition, combustion and volcanoes. Don't draw the respiration arrow from animals only.

notes.b: Dead organisms, faeces and fallen leaves contain a lot of carbon. Decomposers are the living things that break this matter down and return its carbon to the air, so the cycle can keep turning.
points: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi. They feed saprophytically (on dead organic matter): they secrete enzymes that digest the matter outside their cells, absorb the products, and respire them, releasing CO₂ and minerals.
Say that decomposers digest the matter and then respire the products. The CO₂ comes from their respiration, not from the matter breaking down into CO₂ directly.

Without decomposers, carbon would stay locked in dead matter and the CO₂ supply for photosynthesis would run out. There is more on this in Bacteria and fungi, and soil microbiomes are covered in The microbiome.
Decomposers work fastest when it is warm, moist and well aerated, because they respire aerobically (using oxygen).
In cold, waterlogged, acidic or oxygen-poor places decomposition is very slow, so dead matter builds up, e.g. as peat in bogs.

Anaerobic decomposition: where there is no oxygen (waterlogged soils, bogs, rice paddies, landfill, slurry tanks and the stomachs of cattle and sheep), some microorganisms break organic matter down to methane (CH₄) instead of CO₂.
The methane-producing microorganisms are archaea, a separate group of single-celled organisms from bacteria (see Domains of life). Methane in the air is slowly converted to CO₂.
notes.tip: For the role of decomposers, give: they digest dead matter with enzymes, respire the products, release CO₂ for producers, and return minerals. You do not need to name any species.

notes.b: Fossil fuels are a store of carbon that the natural cycle leaves almost untouched. People now burn them, which is why they matter so much to the carbon cycle.
points: Fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas) are the remains of organisms that lived millions of years ago and were buried before they could decompose fully.

Coal formed mainly from land plants in ancient swamps. Oil and natural gas formed mainly from tiny marine organisms (plankton) buried in sea-floor mud. Heat and pressure over millions of years changed them into fuels.

The carbon in fossil fuels was fixed by photosynthesis long ago, so they store ancient solar energy and carbon. Peat is an early stage of the same process, which is why it is sometimes counted with them.
In the natural cycle almost no carbon leaves this store.

Burning fossil fuels since the Industrial Revolution moves carbon locked away for millions of years into the atmosphere in a few centuries, far faster than photosynthesis and the oceans can take it back, so atmospheric CO₂ rises. Consequences are in Climate change and biological strategies.
notes.tip: To explain how fossil fuels formed, say organisms were buried before decomposing and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years. Coal is from plants, oil and gas from marine plankton, not from dinosaurs. To explain why burning raises CO₂, say it releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years.

notes.h: Carbon sinks and sources in the cycle
notes.b: Whether a store helps to lower or raise atmospheric CO₂ depends on whether carbon is flowing in or out. Photosynthesis shows how plants act as sinks; here the sink and source distinction is applied to every store and to the overall balance of the cycle.
points: A store acts as a sink when its inputs exceed its outputs, so it gains carbon, and as a source when its outputs exceed its inputs, so it releases carbon.

The same store can switch between the two: a growing forest is a sink; a mature forest roughly balances; a burning or felled forest is a source. A healthy wet bog is a sink; a drained or burning bog is a source.

The main natural sinks on a carbon-cycle diagram are land plants (forests and grassland, with the soil carbon under them); algae and phytoplankton in the oceans (with dissolving CO₂ and shells sinking to the sea floor); bogs and other wetlands; and limestone and fossil fuels as very long-term stores.
These sinks are compared, and the strategies that use them are described, in Climate change and biological strategies.

Before large-scale fossil-fuel burning, the CO₂ taken up by photosynthesis and the oceans each year was roughly balanced by the CO₂ released by respiration, decomposition and natural fires. Atmospheric CO₂ therefore stayed nearly constant, at about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution.
Deforestation and fossil-fuel burning have tipped this balance, so more CO₂ is now added than removed.

Seasonal pattern: atmospheric CO₂ falls each northern summer, when photosynthesis exceeds respiration over the large land area of the northern hemisphere, and rises each winter, when respiration and decomposition exceed photosynthesis. This happens on top of the long-term rise.
notes.tip: If a graph shows CO₂ rising and falling each year, link the fall to summer photosynthesis and the rise to winter respiration and decomposition, then note the long-term rise underneath.

notes.b: A model represents the cycle in a diagram and in words, and is used to explain and predict. It is only as good as its limits allow.
points: Diagram: draw boxes for the stores: carbon dioxide in the air; green plants and algae; animals; dead organisms and wastes; decomposers (bacteria and fungi); fossil fuels; oceans.

Diagram arrows, each labelled with its process: photosynthesis (air → plants); feeding (plants → animals); death and excretion (plants and animals → dead matter); decomposition (dead matter → decomposers); respiration (plants, animals and decomposers → air).
Diagram arrows, continued: fossilisation (dead matter → fossil fuels, over millions of years); combustion (fossil fuels and wood → air); dissolving (air ↔ oceans).
Prediction (a): cutting down and burning a forest removes photosynthesis and adds combustion and the decomposition of the remains, so atmospheric CO₂ rises.
Prediction (b): draining a bog lets air in, so aerobic decomposers break down the peat and release CO₂.

Prediction (c): if decomposers were killed (e.g. by soil made very acidic or polluted), dead matter would accumulate, minerals would not be returned to the soil, and plant growth would eventually fall.

Limitation: a diagram shows the processes but not how much carbon moves or how fast. It also treats each store as one box, although the oceans, soils and forests each hold carbon for very different lengths of time.
Limitation: it simplifies feedbacks, e.g. warming speeds up decomposition, which releases more CO₂. It is also a snapshot that hides seasonal and long-term change. There is more on this in Models.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to draw or complete the diagram and name the process at a given arrow, then predict the effect of a change such as deforestation or draining a bog. Trace which arrows get bigger or smaller and say what happens to atmospheric CO₂.

keyTerms.definition: The continuous movement of a chemical element between living things and the non-living environment.
A place where carbon is held, such as the atmosphere, the oceans, living organisms, soil, rocks or fossil fuels.
A store whose inputs of carbon exceed its outputs, so that it gains carbon.
A store whose outputs of carbon exceed its inputs, so that it releases carbon.
A bacterium or fungus that digests dead organic matter by secreting enzymes and absorbing the products.
The breakdown of organic matter without oxygen, which releases methane instead of CO₂.
Burning, which combines carbon with oxygen and releases it as CO₂ very quickly.
Coal, oil or natural gas formed from the remains of organisms buried before they could decompose fully.
A process that moves carbon from one store to another.
The burial of dead organic matter, which over millions of years turns it into fossil fuel.

questions.prompt: Name two processes that return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere and one process that removes it. State where each takes place or which organisms carry it out.
questions.model: Two processes that return CO₂ to the atmosphere are respiration, which all organisms carry out, and decomposition by bacteria and fungi in the soil, although combustion of wood, peat or fossil fuels also does so. One process that removes CO₂ is photosynthesis, carried out by green plants, algae and phytoplankton, which fix it into glucose and then into their biomass.

questions.prompt: Model the carbon cycle, with reference to photosynthesis, respiration, decomposers, fossil fuels and carbon sinks. Include a labelled diagram.
questions.model: A labelled diagram shows the stores (carbon dioxide in the air, plants and algae, animals, dead matter, decomposers, fossil fuels and oceans) joined by arrows for photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition, fossilisation, combustion and dissolving. Photosynthesis moves CO₂ from the air into plants and algae, which makes them carbon sinks. Respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns CO₂ to the air. Decomposers, which are bacteria and fungi, digest dead organisms and wastes and respire the products, releasing CO₂ and minerals, so carbon is recycled. Fossil fuels are the remains of organisms buried for millions of years; burning them releases carbon that has been locked away for a very long time, so the cycle is effectively opened and atmospheric CO₂ rises. Sinks are stores whose inputs exceed their outputs, such as growing forests, healthy bogs and the oceans.

questions.prompt: Use your model of the carbon cycle to predict the effect on atmospheric carbon dioxide of draining and cutting a peat bog. Give one limitation of the model.
questions.model: Draining the bog lets air in, so aerobic decomposers break down the peat and release CO₂ into the atmosphere. Cutting the vegetation removes the photosynthesis that was fixing carbon, so the bog changes from a carbon sink to a carbon source, and atmospheric CO₂ rises. One limitation is that the diagram shows the processes but not how much carbon moves or how fast, so it cannot predict the size of the change.
